claims.text: Structural stability of high-entropy nanoalloys at high temperature is governed by formation of a single-phase BCC structure.
Chemical stability of high-entropy nanoalloys at high temperature is governed by formation of a single-phase BCC structure.
A single-phase BCC structure can be achieved through in-situ X-ray diffraction or transmission electron microscopy.
In-situ X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy can characterize phase evolution and stability in high-entropy alloys under extreme or high-temperature conditions.
The proposed structural mediator is formation of a single-phase BCC structure.
A single-phase BCC structure produces thermal stability.
A single-phase BCC structure produces resistance to oxidation and corrosion.
High-entropy nanoalloys will have improved structural stability relative to conventional alloys.
High-entropy nanoalloys will reduce oxidation rates by at least 20% relative to conventional alloys.
High-entropy nanoalloys will reduce corrosion rates by at least 20% relative to conventional alloys.
The prediction is bounded to temperatures from 600 to 900 degrees Celsius.
The relationship between high-entropy composition and formation of the proposed single-phase BCC structure is not fully understood.
Oxidation and corrosion rates can be compared between high-entropy nanoalloys and conventional-alloy controls in a high-temperature environment.
Failure to achieve at least a 20% reduction in oxidation and corrosion rates relative to conventional alloys is defined as falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis treats XRD or TEM characterization as a means of achieving the BCC mediator, whereas the experiment treats these techniques as measurements for observing microstructure. Characterization detects structure but is not presented with any processing action capable of causing BCC formation.
